title: Repair first (2:9)
hookLine: Yom Kippur doesn't clear wrongs against people until they're made right
tomorrow: what if you ask, and they say no?

lines: THE CRACKED SPEAKER. THE SKIPPED SHIFT.
cards: Borrowed a friend's speaker, dropped it, said sorry, handed it back cracked. Promised to cover the shift you ditched and never did. Said something about someone that's still making the rounds.
Lists like that pile up, and a big holy day can start to look like a reset button. Does a holy day clear a wrong you never fixed? Maimonides answers flatly, and the answer is no.
Not the ones against people. Not yet.

teach.b: He splits wrongs in two. Some are between a person and God alone. For those, return and Yom Kippur bring atonement.

The others are between people: hurting someone, taking what's theirs, shaming them. For those, he writes, there is no forgiveness until the person gives back what they owe, and then wins the other one over.
Two steps, and he means both.
Paying back isn't enough on its own; you still have to make peace and ask.
And words count. Even if all you did was hurt someone with what you said, you go to them and keep at it until they forgive you. He didn't invent this.

The Mishnah teaches it in the name of Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah: Yom Kippur covers what's between a person and God, but what's between a person and another person, Yom Kippur doesn't cover until the other is set right.

So the Day of Atonement itself comes with a to-do list that only the injured person can sign off. That's why, in some homes, the days before Yom Kippur fill with phone calls and awkward knocks on doors.
Repair first, then the fast does its work.

how: Before Yom Kippur some Jews call or visit friends and family to ask forgiveness for anything they did in the past year, following the teaching that the day doesn't clear wrongs between people until they're set right.

o: fix your own heart before you fix the harm
fix the harm to a person before the holy day
fast first, then the wrongs are cleared

games.q: two kinds of wrong — tap the pairs.
p: win the person over and ask

s: Yom Kippur wipes the whole slate, including wrongs against people
Maimonides and the Mishnah: wrongs between people wait until the person is set right.
paying back what you owe is enough on its own
Maimonides adds a second step: make peace with the person and ask their forgiveness.
even hurtful words need repair before the day can clear them
if you only hurt someone with words, you still go to them and keep at it until they forgive.

games.q: backing out of the driveway, you crushed your neighbor's trash bin. you called 'so sorry!' over the fence and drove off. by Maimonides, what's still owed?
o: a new bin, and a real conversation asking them to forgive you.
nothing; the sorry was sincere, and that settles a small thing.
a quiet confession on Yom Kippur, which covers small accidents.
games.why: between people, it's two steps: give back what's owed, then win the person over. the holy day waits for both.

practice: Pick up your phone and open a message to someone you owe a repair: a thing returned, a debt paid, a word unsaid. Write it plainly, what you'll make right and when.
You don't have to send it during the sit; just let the version sit there, finished, while you breathe.

wordCard.voice: Repair first: Yom Kippur doesn't clear wrongs against people until they're made right. Give back what's owed, then win the person over.

orig.note: Hebrew: the Day of Atonement, Yom Kippur.

carryVoice: Carry this: repair first, since the holy day waits for the person you hurt. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Teshuvah 2:9 (wrongs between people not forgiven until paid back and appeased; even words)
Mishnah Yoma 8:9 (Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah: Yom Kippur atones between a person and God, not between people until appeased)
